summary: This UF/IFAS Extension publication (CIR1082) by Gary D. Butcher and Richard D. Miles is a starter guide for beginning pet bird owners on bird nutrition. It explains the six nutrient classes (water, proteins, carbohydrates and fiber, lipids, minerals, vitamins), argues that balanced or complete diets are best, and warns that seed-only diets, excess treats, and excess protein cause deficiencies, obesity, and organ damage. It recommends feeding variety from four food groups if a balanced pellet diet is not possible.
one_line: UF/IFAS guide explaining the six nutrient classes and why pet birds need balanced, varied diets rather than seed-only feeding.
key_facts: The publication CIR1082 by Gary D. Butcher and Richard D. Miles was released June 4, 2018 and reviewed January 6, 2022.
The note states there are six major categories of nutrients: water, proteins, carbohydrates, lipids, minerals, and vitamins.
A 10% loss of body water can cause serious illness in a pet bird, and without replacement of lost water, death will result.
Of the 22 amino acids required by animals, about 12 can be made in animal cells and the other 10 must be consumed in the diet.
Usually plant proteins are deficient in the amino acids methionine and lysine with regard to a pet bird's requirement.
Fats and oils furnish 2.25 times more calories of energy per unit weight than carbohydrates and proteins.
Cellulose cannot furnish energy to pet birds because animals do not produce the enzyme cellulase.
Seeds contain only 200 to 500 parts per million (0.02 to 0.05 percent) calcium, while the growing bird requirement is close to 1 percent of the diet.
Sunflower seeds contain 8 parts phosphorus to every part calcium.
The note says the fat soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K can become toxic in large amounts, a condition called hypervitaminosis.
Overfortification with vitamins A and D should be of major concern, according to the note.
Only microorganisms can make vitamin B12; animal tissues and products such as milk and eggs contain it.
The note states that pet birds can be fed all-seed diets for many years before they begin to look unhealthy.
Excess protein can damage the liver and kidney, and fat birds are subject to liver and pancreas problems.
The note says there are more than 8000 species of birds alive today.
